documents.abstract: Although the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming educational guidance and career counselling, its impact on quality and professionalism has not been sufficiently researched. This scoping review investigates how AI influences counselling methods and professional standards and analyses 20 publications (2015–2025) from two databases (ERIC and German Education Index) using a systematic micro-, meso-, and macro-level framework. Although research in this area has grown rapidly since 2022, concrete quality standards for AI-supported counsel­ling remain elusive. While AI can simulate empathy and provide reflective prompts, it cannot replicate genuine human warmth or address complex biographical issues. Acknowledging AI’s potential to enhance accessibility, it only serves as an expansion of the repertoire rather than a replacement for human reflexivity. In order to safeguard professional integrity in the postdigital era, the study recommends implementing mandatory AI competencies and establishing a digital commons infrastructure to protect counselling values from commercial interests.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Music is a distinctly human artform, one that has been written, taught, shared, and reinterpreted for thousands of years. The rise of powerful artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping musical creation in ways subtle and profound. Here I propose the human-AI performance loop as a framework for understanding these developments through three principal roles: the AI listener derives musical information from sound and movement; the AI coach guides practice using performance evidence and musicians’ learning goals; and the AI partner performs with the musician in a collaborative dynamic process. With the human musician at the centre of the framework, human → AI → human exchanges become coupled through shared information and musicians’ actions. Evaluating these roles will require multilayered evidence to support their adoption: accurate and musically relevant analysis, demonstrated improvements in musician performance and knowledge through coaching, and effective and supportive coordination between musicians and AI partners. Audience beliefs about AI will also shape reception of the creative output, making musical purpose and honest representation important considerations in an AI music performance system. The human-AI performance loop provides a basis for investigating how these roles can extend support between lessons and rehearsals, broaden opportunities for ensemble performance, and contribute to musicians’ learning and enjoyment of the musical experience.

This article examines the potential of artificial intelligence to reduce judicial pendency in India without compromising human judgment. It explores existing applications, including SUPACE, SUVAS and eCourts Phase III, alongside judicial concerns regarding fabricated citations, algorithmic bias and automation bias. Through an analysis of relevant Indian judicial decisions, the article distinguishes AI-assisted research and administrative functions from adjudicatory decision-making. It argues that AI should complement, rather than replace, judicial reasoning through mandatory human verification, independent assessment of legal authorities and accountable use. The article concludes that responsible integration of AI can improve judicial efficiency while preserving fairness, accuracy and legitimacy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The research paper titled “AI Smart Study Assistant Using Large Language Models and AI Agents” proposes a conceptual framework for personalized and intelligent learning. It integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and specialized AI agents to provide students with question answering, note summarization, quiz generation, study planning, and personalized revision recommendations. The system uses course materials and student quiz performance to generate context-aware learning support and identify topics requiring further practice. The proposed framework aims to make learning more organized, interactive, and efficient while highlighting challenges such as response accuracy, privacy, and agent coordination.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This paper develops a framework for an AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison course by bringing together Byram’s intercultural communicative competence model, Vygotsky’s constructivism, and Huang et al.’s theory of cultural competence development. It identifies five interrelated course goals: cultural knowledge, cross-cultural practical ability, critical cultural awareness, AI collaboration literacy, and human-AI symbiosis awareness. To achieve these goals, three teaching strategies are proposed. First, content should be reconstructed through multimodal and professionally adapted resources; second, the learning process should be immersive and adaptive; third, assessment should be data-driven and multidimensional to evaluate the goals. The implementation conditions of these strategies are further discussed in terms of teacher AI competence, human-AI boundary negotiation, algorithmic bias mitigation, and differentiated task design. It provides a structured basis for AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison teaching and for future empirical testing of its effects.

The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education has transformed how business and management subjects are taught and learned. In finance education, traditional teaching methods often emphasize numerical calculations and theoretical frameworks while offering limited opportunities for experiential and behavioral learning. In this case study, the authors present a real classroom-based pedagogical intervention implemented in a course for undergraduate and postgraduate students at Commerce and Management Institutes in India, where AI tools and behavioral finance simulations through games were integrated into teaching practices to improve student engagement, analytical thinking, and practical decision-making skills. This case study emerged from observations by the teaching faculty who taught Behavioural Finance courses to undergraduate and graduate students, who frequently struggled to connect financial theories with real-world investment behaviour and market psychology. In an attempt to make students show their interest in learning this kind of course, which requires understanding the fundamentals of Psychology, which is a prerequisite for this course. To address these challenges, AI-assisted simulations, AI-generated market scenarios, interactive case discussions, and behavioural finance activities were introduced into the classroom in the form of a game. Students were exposed to emotionally driven financial decision-making situations, such as panic selling, herding behaviour, overconfidence bias, and speculative investment trends, through AI-generated business narratives and stock market simulations. The teaching faculty made an attempt through gamification as an intervention by adopting a simulation-based learning framework. Based on the authors' experience in teaching behavioural finance courses, a simulation was created using AI. This AI-generated investment simulation scenario was used as a pilot study in the real classroom. The students actively participated in games and were able to make decisions rather than absorb theoretical content. AI tools were used to generate realistic market situations, investment dilemmas, and personalised learning prompts that encouraged critical analysis and collaborative problem-solving. The results demonstrated and presented active classroom participation, improved conceptual understanding, enhanced critical thinking abilities, and greater student interest in finance subjects. Students reported that the integration of AI made finance learning more relatable, practical, and interactive. This case also discusses ethical concerns, faculty adaptation challenges, limitations of AI-generated learning environments, and recommendations for responsible AI integration in finance education. This case study contributes to the growing discourse on gamification through AI-enabled pedagogy by demonstrating how behavioural finance and AI can be combined to create immersive and mock experiential learning experiences in management education.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Innovative approaches are needed to deliver secure software, as software systems grow in complexity and cyber threats become more sophisticated. Most of the traditional security mechanisms cannot keep track of dynamic attacks, exposing vulnerabilities that a hacker can use. Deep learning models of artificial intelligence (AI) provide an effective solution through their autonomy in the detection and mitigation of threats. In this paper, we present an approach to AI-augmented secure software engineering, demonstrating the ways in which deep learning techniques can augment security practices in each stage of the software development lifecycle. First, we focus on the constraints of traditional security architectures based on static rulebased systems and human decision-making power. Next, we discuss AI-based approaches like DNNs/CNNs/RNNs to support real-time anomaly detection, code vulnerability examinations, and intelligent threat predictions. By analyzing large volumes of data and identifying patterns that may suggest cyber threats, these models can respond to security incidents automatically, minimizing human effort and increasing accuracy in detection. Additionally, it highlights how deep learning is being leveraged in the DevSecOps pipeline to proactively enforce security through continuous monitoring and automated patching. We examine practical instances among which are adversarial learning methods for malware detection, reinforcement learningbased techniques for intrusion prevention, and large volume threat intelligence collection and analysis. While AI has the potential to bring about incredible change, ongoing challenges in areas like model explainability, adversarial AI, and ethical and regulatory concerns must be addressed. Through the use of AI-based technologies, software engineering can evolve from passive (reactive) security paradigms to self-adaptive (proactive) architectures that bolster robustness against cyberattacks. Through this work, we advance the state-of-the-art in AIbased security systems by introducing a framework that can robustly cross-focus on safety aspects, highlighting the commonalities between deep learning approaches and secure software engineering that can aid in building stronger, self-governing countermeasures.

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of global mortality, with acute events such as myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac arrest often occurring without sufficient prehospital warning. Advances in wearable sensor technology and edgecomputing Artificial Intelligence (AI) have enabled non-invasive, continuous monitoring of multi-parameter physiological signals, including Electrocardiogram (ECG), Photoplethysmogram (PPG), Heart Rate Variability (HRV), Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO2), and Skin Temperature. This review evaluates existing paradigms for automated cardiac arrhythmia detection, ischemic risk profiling, and emergency response dispatch. The primary foundational methodology examined leverages a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network and Long Short-Term Memory Network (1D-CNN-LSTM) paired with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAI / SHAP) for model interpretability. Evaluated across benchmark datasets including PhysioNet MIT-BIH Arrhythmia and the PTB-XL ECG Database, the hybrid deep learning architecture achieves a classification accuracy of 98.42% for multiclass arrhythmia detection and ischemic episode classification. Beyond single-lead ECG analysis, this paper reviews self-supervised representation learning and multi-sensor fusion models designed to mitigate motion artifacts and signal loss in free-living environments. Based on the reviewed literature, a critical research gap is identified: existing wearable solutions treat risk detection and emergency escalation as isolated processes, lacking real-time localized edge inference paired with explainable clinical decision-support. To address this, we propose an end-to-end framework combining multi-parameter wearable sensor data, edge-deployed Lightweight MobileNet-LSTM networks, Explainable AI (XAI) feature attribution, automated dynamic risk scoring, and automated emergency alert escalation with GPS location tracking.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

documents.abstract: Traffic jams become a frequent issue in rapidly growing cities; however, the time-fixed lights do not adjust properly to changing car traffic. In this paper, different approaches using the following elements: artificial intelligence, computer vision, reinforcement learning, deep learning, and Internet of Things have been discussed in the field of traffic control. With these methods, traffic can be detected and adjusted for in real time. However, there are several issues which should be resolved in the future, such as bad weather conditions, different traffic, high computational requirements, and others.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and generative models has created new opportunities for automating creative processes, particularly in music composition and audio production. Traditional music creation often requires musical knowledge, instrument-playing skills, professional audio-editing tools, and considerable time. These requirements can make music production challenging for beginners and individuals without formal musical training. To address these challenges, this research proposes an AI-Based Voice-to-Music Generation System that enables users to create musical compositions through natural voice commands. The proposed system aims to integrate speech recognition, natural language processing, audio signal processing, and AI-based music generation into a unified framework. Users can provide voice commands through a microphone or upload audio recordings describing their musical preferences. The system processes the input using speech recognition techniques to convert speech into text. Natural Language Processing is then applied to identify relevant musical characteristics, including genre, mood, tempo, and instrument preferences. Based on the extracted information, an appropriate generative music model produces a musical composition corresponding to the user's instructions. The generated audio is subsequently processed and made available for playback, saving, and downloading through an interactive user interface. The effectiveness of the proposed system will be investigated through experiments evaluating speech recognition accuracy, musical command interpretation, music generation quality, processing time, and user satisfaction. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Voice-to-Music Generation, Natural Language Processing, Speech Recognition, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Generative Music Models, Audio Signal Processing, Music Composition.

The growing complexity of global food systems and the burden of foodborne diseases highlight limitations in conventional food safety approaches based on retrospective testing and isolated analytical measurements. High-throughput omics technologies, including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and microbiomics, enable comprehensive molecular characterization of food systems, but their scale and heterogeneity challenge conventional analytical approaches. Artificial Intelligence (AI) can integrate these heterogeneous datasets to support predictive food-safety, quality-assurance, and risk-assessment applications. This review provides a critical overview of AI-enabled multi-omics integration for food safety, covering major omics platforms, multimodal integration, machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), graph neural networks (GNNs), transformer-based approaches, and explainable AI (XAI). Applications include pathogen detection and characterization, antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) surveillance, shelf-life and spoilage prediction, food authenticity assessment, and risk assessment. Reported results include 0.94 accuracy ( κ = 0.82 ) for genomic prediction of Salmonella disease-endpoint phenotypes, AUROC of 0.904 for Salmonella stress-response prediction, and R 2 > 0.96 for neural-network-based shelf-life prediction. However, performance remains dependent on data quality, model design, and validation strategy. Key challenges include data standardization, missing modalities, batch effects, model interpretability, regulatory acceptance, computational scalability, and limited availability of well-characterized multi-omics food-safety datasets. Emerging directions such as biological foundation models, digital twins, and cyber-physical systems are discussed as longer-term opportunities, while autonomous food-safety management remains an emerging research direction.

Generative AI now produces advertising copy, images and video at a fraction of the cost and time of human creative work, and the quality of its output is often indistinguishable from human-created content. What consumers make of it, once they know, is less clear. This paper examines perceived brand authenticity across three ad-creation conditions, human-created, AI-generated without disclosure and AI-generated with disclosure, in a comparative simulation of 1,200 consumers that also varies brand type. AI-generated content undisclosed lowers perceived authenticity modestly (0.65 to 0.59) despite slightly higher execution quality; disclosure lowers it substantially (to 0.43), and the penalty is larger for heritage brands (0.38) than for non-heritage brands (0.48). Brand attitude follows authenticity, so that disclosed AI content yields the lowest attitude despite the highest quality. The paper interprets the results through brand authenticity theory, in which authenticity rests on perceived genuineness, origin and craft, argues that AI generation threatens the origin and craft components in proportion to how central they are to the brand, and derives guidance on where AI content fits, how disclosure should be handled under emerging transparency requirements, and how brands can preserve authenticity while using generative tools.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Ageing infrastructure requires continuous monitoring to identify early signs of structural damage and prevent potential failures. Conventional inspection methods rely primarily on manual observation, making them time-consuming, costly, and difficult to perform frequently. This paper presents an Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things (AI-IoT)-based structural health monitoring system that integrates computer vision and vibration sensing for automated crack detection and abnormal vibration identification. A camera captures images of the monitored structure, and a lightweight MobileNetV2-based deep learning model classifies surface conditions as crack or no-crack. Simultaneously, an L3G4200D gyroscope interfaced with a Raspberry Pi provides angular velocity readings, which are analysed using a calibrated threshold-based method to identify deviations from baseline vibration conditions. A rule-based fusion engine combines the visual and sensor outputs to classify the overall structural condition into three severity levels: LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH. An RGB LED provides local status indication, while a secure web dashboard enables remote monitoring of structural conditions. When a HIGH-severity condition is detected, the system generates an automated email alert to facilitate timely inspection and corrective action. The proposed system demonstrates the integration of AI-based vision, IoT sensing, severity assessment, and automated alerts for structural condition monitoring. Further quantitative evaluation and real-world validation are required to establish its reliability and practical applicability

The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), and electromyography (EMG) has enabled the development of next-generation rehabilitation systems that are adaptive, data-driven, and patient-centered. This systematic review synthesizes recent advances (2020–2026) in integrated AI-powered VR rehabilitation frameworks utilizing EMG signals. Following a structured review methodology, 17 studies were analyzed with respect to machine learning techniques, system architectures, sensing modalities, and evaluation practices. Several studies reported high within-subject classification performance, whereas subject-independent generalization remained more challenging where it was directly evaluated. However, the reported performance estimates were obtained from heterogeneous datasets, participant groups, movement sets, sensor configurations, and validation protocols and should therefore be interpreted as study-specific feasibility results rather than directly compared across studies. The integration of multimodal biosignals enables real-time assessment of user states, including fatigue and stress, facilitating closed-loop adaptive rehabilitation. Despite these technical advancements, only a minority of studies involved clinical populations. Key challenges include inter-subject variability, small sample sizes, lack of longitudinal evaluation, and limited generalizability of trained models. Emerging approaches such as transfer learning, multimodal sensor fusion, and real-time adaptive control show promise in addressing these limitations.

In Katsina State, Nigeria, this study created and assessed CassavaGuard AI, an offline Android software for image-based cassava mosaic disease (CMD) screening. The program makes use of a pretrained MobileNetV3-Small network that has been compressed using static INT8 post-training quantization and adjusted for four operational leaf-image classes. Training (5,915), validation (1,268), and holdout test (1,267) sets were created from an 8,450 image dataset. The model obtained a macro F1-score of 92.45% and an accuracy of 92.58% on the holdout test set. The model file size was decreased from 21.4 MB to 5.9 MB using quantization. Total image-processing time was 42.6 ms on the Tecno Spark 8P and 58.4 ms on the 2 GB Infinix Hot 10i; peak application memory use was 145 MB. The usability assessment involved 45 farmers and 15 agricultural extension officers. The group mean System Usability Scale (SUS) scores were 87.75 and 94.00, respectively, giving a weighted overall score of 89.31/100; this calculation should be checked against the original questionnaire records. The study integrates on-device classification, local record storage, optional synchronization, and Hausa–English user support. The findings indicate the potential of lightweight deep learning for offline cassava disease screening on low-cost smartphones, although independent validation is needed before wider deployment

This article proposes an evidence-informed adaptive model for improving university educators’ professional practice in digitally mediated teaching. Drawing on DigCompEdu, TPACK, UNESCO guidance on artificial intelligence and design-based educational inquiry, it defines five competence domains and links them to observable teaching artefacts. The proposed cycle covers diagnosis, contextual interpretation, co-designed professional learning, implementation and reassessment. An engineering-computer-graphics scenario illustrates its practical relevance, while an evaluation protocol specifies how future research could test its validity, feasibility and outcomes. As the available materials lack auditable experimental datasets, no causal or numerical effectiveness claims are advanced. The contribution is an integrated framework for formative development under human oversight and responsible data governance

This study presents a human-centred sitting monitoring system that moves beyond discrete posture classification by estimating a continuous Healthy Sitting Score (HSS, 0–100) from electro-textile sensing data. Forty-eight tactile features were used with PINNR, SVR, and GPR models, and generalization was evaluated using participant-wise Group Cross-Validation and an independent unseen-subject test set. The best PINNR model achieved R = 0.948, R² = 0.898, and RMSE = 6.83 on unseen participants. The system was integrated with a Bluetooth-enabled Android application providing real-time HSS visualization, history, summaries, and configurable notifications. In a 21-participant workplace evaluation, usability ratings were high and HSS increased significantly after the first notification, although the absence of a no-feedback control limits causal interpretation. Repeated-use analysis over 21 workdays showed no widespread sensor drift. Overall, the study emphasizes continuous posture-quality scoring, personalized feedback, behavioural response, and real-world HCI evaluation rather than multi-class posture recognition.

This is a case study update on the design, delivery and performance of a first-year undergraduate statistics subject (or course/unit/module), entitled Making Sense of Data, at La Trobe University. This subject is taught both face-to-face and online to a large cohort of students across a number of domestic and international campuses. In order to support the diverse educational backgrounds and chosen qualifications of students, Making Sense of Data contains both a solid foundation of core statistics content, and a stream-specific component. All students cover the core content, and the stream content that best aligns with their chosen qualification(s). This flexible, accessible structure helps ensure that the subject’s intended learning outcomes are met whilst highlighting the relevance of statistics for each student’s field of study and allowing for stream-specific lectures, assessments and statistical software to be used. In this paper we discuss various feedback-based refinements implemented iteratively in Making Sense of Data in recent years, including adjustments to classes, learning content, assessments, and student support, as well as adjustments made in response to the emergence of Generative AI. We evaluate how these changes to the subject have impacted student outcomes in terms of engagement, satisfaction and performance.

As workforce aging and artificial intelligence (AI) applications increasingly unfold in parallel, understanding how technological change reshapes older workers' adaptive processes and work attitudes has become critical. Drawing on selection, optimization, and compensation theory, this study introduces anticipatory obsolescence, the specific forward-looking perception of human capital depreciation that is distinct from general job insecurity, as a key conceptual lens for understanding the moderating role of AI-job substitution risk on the relationships between workplace opportunities and successful aging at work. Using data from 1449 workers aged 50 and over in the 9th wave of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe , we examine the relationships linking workplace opportunities for new skills acquisition, job advancement, and job support with job satisfaction as a critical indicator of successful aging at work in the context of AI-related changes. Overall, all three types of opportunities are positively associated with job satisfaction. However, under high AI-job substitution risks, the effect of new skill acquisition is weakened, and the effect of job advancement is strengthened, while no significant moderation effect is observed for the relationship between job support and job satisfaction. This study contributes to scholarships by bridging macro-level objective indicators of AI-induced employment risks to micro-level subjective perception about future human capital value. We offer a nuanced understanding of change-related implications for the aging workforce and practical insights for supporting successful aging of the graying workforce.

topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Abstract This chapter introduces the UX process as a structured, iterative framework for creating user-centered digital products. Readers learn the five core stages—Discover, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test—and how each stage builds on the last. Rather than presenting the process as rigid or linear, the chapter emphasizes iteration, collaboration, and evidence-based decision making. It explains how UX professionals gather insights, define problems, generate solutions, and refine designs through repeated cycles of feedback. The chapter also situates the UX process within its historical foundations in human factors and human–computer interaction (HCI), showing how decades of research shaped modern practice. By the end, readers understand how the UX process guides teams from research to launch and why research, iteration, and testing are essential to successful design.

Abstract The United States Air Force seeks to develop “Collaborative Combat Aircraft” to provide an affordable force multiplier. Current Artificial Intelligence (AI) research efforts often focus on developing the AI necessary to support task work within target domains without sufficiently considering integration in existing systems, including the capabilities necessary to enable the teamwork required to enable human-AI teams. The current research employs a recently published team-oriented analysis and design method, referred to as Agent-Oriented Systems Modeling (AOSM), to provide an architecture-level analysis of the human-AI team to establish requirements for the AI systems in both manned and unmanned aircraft. The approach is applied to an F-16 formation performing defensive counter air, to evaluate task and teamwork requirements within the analogous system. These requirements, namely the goals, responsibilities, and capabilities of the agents in the existing system are then applied to envision the “To-Be” system to ensure equivalent or greater capabilities exist in the proposed architecture. This analysis produces numerous traceable findings that can be applied to establish system level requirements for future development to ensure effective human-AI teaming, including 45 capabilities required of the system and five agent roles to be fulfilled in the “To-Be” system. The project discusses and supports the importance of efficient communication and coordination mechanisms for all AI agents when teaming with the human pilot.

Transformations associated with digital culture and the expansion of Artificial Intelligence have intensified debates about the role of teachers and the nature of pedagogical decision-making. This article aims to propose and theoretically ground Learning Architecture as a theoretical-pedagogical perspective for understanding teaching practice, articulating intentionality, experience, interaction, meaning-making, and authorship. This qualitative, theoretical-conceptual, and interpretive study draws on research on learning, teacher agency, digital culture, and Artificial Intelligence in Education. Pedagogical decision-making is proposed as the transversal axis of the construct, guiding the organization of conditions for learning. The study concludes that technologies, methodologies, and AI systems do not occupy the center of the architecture, but function as resources subordinated to teachers’ educational purposes and pedagogical decisions.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into organizational activities, including information processing, forecasting, customer management, resource allocation, and managerial decision-making. However, the organizational value of AI depends not only on technological adoption but also on how effectively managers collaborate with AI systems and understand their capabilities and limitations. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and managerial decision-making, with particular attention to human–AI collaboration and managerial AI literacy. The proposed framework considers AI adoption as the independent variable, human–AI collaboration as a mediating mechanism, managerial AI literacy as a moderating variable, and managerial decision-making quality, decision-making speed, and organizational performance as outcome variables. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was adopted. Data were obtained from 200 respondents associated with the real-estate and construction ecosystem, including customers/property buyers, managers, engineers, architects, supervisors, labour personnel, brokers, investors, bankers, finance and accounting personnel, HR professionals, administrative staff, sales and marketing personnel, legal and compliance personnel, drivers, security personnel, cleaners, technicians, and other relevant stakeholders. Responses were measured using a five-point Likert scale. Based on the response distribution supplied for the present study, 180 respondents (90%) selected 5 (Strongly Agree) and 20 respondents (10%) selected 4 (Agree) for each reported questionnaire item. The resulting item-level mean was 4.90, indicating a strongly positive response pattern. The study provides a structured framework for examining how AI adoption, human–AI collaboration, and managerial AI literacy may jointly contribute to managerial decision-making and organizational performance. Respondent-level inferential analysis using PLS-SEM is required before reporting path coefficients, mediation, moderation, significance levels, and explained variance.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing rapidly with new tools and capabilities emerging quickly. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) utilize AI in clinical practice, but it is unclear how SLPs use AI tools and the factors that SLPs consider in their decision making. This study presents a survey of school-based SLPs to (a) document the extent and nature of AI use; (b) assess the perceived quality and general opinions of AI; (c) identify ethical, legal, and institutional factors influencing their decisions; and (d) identify the types of AI training currently used and the training SLPs report wanting to receive. Method: Two hundred fourteen school-based SLPs across Ohio completed a survey about the types of AI tools they use, the factors influencing their use, general opinions about AI, and specific concerns about the use of AI in the workplace. The sample was predominantly White (91.3%) and female (97.1%). The average age was 45.17 years, with 19.72 years of professional experience. Participants who used AI within the last 6 months were categorized as “AI users” compared to “non-AI users” who had not. Results: School-based SLPs reported using AI often in their practice across a wide range of tasks. SLPs reported concerns about accuracy or reliability, and ethical concerns as reasons for limiting or not using AI tools. Perceptions of AI quality were mixed, with SLPs divided on whether AI could produce outputs similar to an average practitioner. SLPs reported a significant need for guidance and training in AI tools and ethics. Conclusion: The results highlight the need for clear guidance on the use of AI tools, including ethical implications, along with additional training for school-based SLPs. Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from isolated experimentation toward more embedded use in Vietnam’s banking sector, but the depth of adoption and the quality of public performance evidence remain uneven. This article examines current practices, implementation constraints, and governance priorities through a structured qualitative review updated to 24 August 2026. The review combines peer-reviewed banking research, international risk-governance guidance, Vietnamese legal and supervisory documents, and recent official disclosures from major commercial banks. The evidence indicates that digital identity and biometric authentication are operational and strongly regulation-driven, while machine-learning applications in underwriting, personalization, fraud monitoring, and decision support are increasingly embedded at leading banks. Generative AI has also moved beyond experimentation in several institutions, although sector-wide maturity remains uneven. Recent disclosures provide more concrete operational metrics than earlier sources, but most remain self-reported and cannot establish causal effects on profitability or risk. The main constraints concern fragmented data and legacy integration, model and conduct risk, cybersecurity and third-party dependence, uneven governance capacity, and shortages of interdisciplinary expertise. The article applies a technology–organization–environment framework with a cross-cutting AI-risk governance layer and proposes a sequenced implementation matrix for banks and supervisors. The central implication is that the value of AI in banking depends less on acquiring models than on integrating data, controls, accountable ownership, and human oversight throughout the AI lifecycle.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into policing, welfare administration, employment, credit, education, healthcare, judicial and legal systems, and public administration. Algorithmic systems may improve efficiency, consistency and the processing of large quantities of information, but they may also reproduce or amplify discriminatory patterns embedded in historical data and institutional practices. Where governmental decisions affecting individuals are informed or generated by algorithms, constitutional concerns arise regarding equality, non-discrimination, privacy, dignity, autonomy, freedom, procedural fairness and access to remedies. India does not presently possess a single comprehensive AI-specific constitutional accountability framework. Nevertheless, Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution, together with administrative-law principles and the emerging data-protection and responsible-AI framework, provide a substantial foundation for regulating rights-affecting AI. This paper argues for a rights-based, risk-sensitive Indian framework incorporating algorithmic impact assessment, transparency, meaningful explanation, human oversight, independent auditing, institutional accountability and effective remedies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) together with medical robotics is reshaping the medical field by the production of systems that are more intelligent, adaptable and patient-centric. This chapter focuses on the essential concepts, scientific breakthroughs and clinical applications of AI and ML in medical robotics. The primary topics cover robotic-assisted surgery, diagnostic automation, rehabilitation systems and intelligent patient monitoring. AI and ML empower healthcare interventions with robotic systems accuracy, independence and customization through real-time data analysis, pattern recognition and adaptive decision-making. This chapter also addresses the ethical issues, data privacy concerns and regulatory frameworks that accompany these innovations. By presenting a comprehensive review of the current capabilities and challenges, this chapter aims to be a source of valuable insight for the researchers, clinicians and developers working at the intersection of robotics, artificial intelligence and healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding periodontal care from isolated image interpretation toward integrated, patient specific decision support. Current applications include automated detection and quantification of alveolar bone loss, periodontitis classification, prediction of treatment response, assistance with treatment planning, remote behavioural monitoring and measurement of peri implant bone changes. The field has advanced rapidly, and 2025-2026 studies increasingly examine multimodal models that combine radiographs, intraoral scans and clinical records. Nevertheless, most evidence remains retrospective, single-centre and dependent on heterogeneous definitions and reference standards. High accuracy in a selected dataset does not establish clinical readiness, generalizability or benefit to patients. This narrative review explains the principal AI methods used in periodontics, evaluates their roles across diagnosis, prognosis, therapy and supportive care, and proposes a practical pathway for responsible implementation. The most defensible current use of AI is augmentation: standardizing repetitive measurements, organizing complex information, displaying uncertainty and supporting communication while the periodontist retains responsibility for examination, diagnosis and shared decision-making. Future progress requires representative multicentre datasets, external and prospective validation, calibrated predictions, transparent reporting, privacy protection, subgroup evaluation, interoperable records and evidence that AI-assisted workflows improve periodontal outcomes without widening inequality. When governed appropriately, AI may become an important component of precision periodontics, but it should complement rather than replace clinical expertise.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across reproductive medicine, including semen analysis, sperm detection and selection, oocyte and embryo assessment, prediction of assisted reproductive technology outcomes, clinical decision support, and integration of multi-omics data. Large language models and generative AI are also emerging as tools for scientific writing, education, documentation, and research support. This review critically examines the current applications, clinical readiness, and research-integrity implications of AI in reproductive medicine. Although many models demonstrate promising performance in classification, ranking, or outcome prediction, the available evidence remains predominantly retrospective, task-specific, and derived from single-center or internally validated datasets. High technical performance does not necessarily translate into improved cumulative live birth, patient safety, cost-effectiveness, workflow efficiency, or equitable clinical outcomes. Important barriers include dataset heterogeneity, limited external and prospective validation, inadequate calibration assessment, data leakage, algorithmic bias, limited interpretability, privacy and cybersecurity risks, and vulnerability to performance drift. Generative AI introduces additional concerns, including fabricated references, inaccurate scientific summaries, undisclosed contributions, confidentiality breaches, and the generation or alteration of images that may be misrepresented as empirical evidence. Responsible translation therefore requires transparent reporting, independent temporal and geographic validation, subgroup and fairness analyses, prospective clinical-impact evaluation, preservation of data and model provenance, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Current international guidance further emphasizes that AI systems cannot qualify as authors and that accountable human researchers must verify generated content and disclose material AI use. AI should presently be regarded as an assistive technology that augments, rather than replaces, embryologists, clinicians, and researchers. Future progress will depend on multicenter prospective studies using patient-important outcomes, design-appropriate reporting frameworks, risk-based regulatory oversight, and clearly defined human accountability throughout the AI lifecycle.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background. Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability, and rehabilitation led by physical therapy is central to recovery. In Nigeria, rehabilitation is limited by few specialized services, uneven geographical distribution of health workers and facilities, and weak follow-up and data systems. These problems affect how progress is assessed, monitored and continued after hospital discharge, and they raise the question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) could help. Objective. To review how AI might support physical therapy and stroke rehabilitation in Nigeria, and to examine the opportunities, limitations, ethical considerations and implementation challenges. Review approach. This is a narrative literature review of existing academic and institutional evidence. It is not a systematic review and involved no original data collection or AI development. International, other African and Nigerian evidence is distinguished throughout. Main findings. International reviews describe AI applications in movement and gait assessment, outcome prediction, exercise monitoring and remote rehabilitation, with promising but uneven evidence. A mapping review found that external validation and explainability were rarely reported (Morone et al., 2025). No Nigerian evaluation of AI-assisted stroke rehabilitation was identified among the literature reviewed. Nigerian evidence relates mainly to rehabilitation access, feasibility of low-technology telerehabilitation and the state of stroke services and data. Barriers include unreliable power and connectivity, cost, workforce training, data quality, privacy and the under-representation of African populations in AI development. Conclusion. AI has potential to support more personalized assessment, monitoring, decision support, use of rehabilitation data and continuity of care. It should augment, not replace, physical therapists. Realistic progress in Nigeria depends on local evidence, infrastructure, training, data quality, privacy protection, affordability, equity and human clinical oversight.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool for improving decision-making across fruit production and postharvest management. However, evidence regarding its applications, reported performance, and practical limitations remains distributed across different fruit crops, sensing technologies, and computational approaches. This review systematically examines the applications of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, robotics, the Internet of Things (IoT), and remote sensing in fruit science. Relevant publications were identified through searches of [databases used] covering the period from [start year] to [end year], using predefined search terms and eligibility criteria. Of the [number] records identified, [number] studies were included in the final synthesis. The selected literature was categorised into precision orchard management, pest and disease detection, fruit detection and yield estimation, robotic harvesting, non-destructive quality assessment, and postharvest handling. The synthesis compares the reported performance of AI models, their application across fruit crops, the sensing technologies employed, and the principal limitations affecting field implementation. Particular attention is given to quantitative outcomes reported for detection accuracy, prediction performance, harvesting efficiency, resource use, and fruit quality assessment. The review also evaluates challenges associated with dataset availability, model generalization, computational requirements, sensor integration, and deployment under variable orchard conditions. Emerging approaches, including edge AI, multimodal data fusion, explainable AI, and autonomous orchard systems, are discussed in relation to the limitations identified in existing studies. By connecting reported experimental outcomes with implementation constraints, this review identifies evidence-based research priorities for developing reliable and scalable AI applications in fruit production and postharvest management.

This research examines the effectiveness of artificial intelligence as a cybersecurity support tool for nontechnical users. The study evaluated ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude 3 across five simulated cybersecurity scenarios involving phishing attempts, password reuse, fraudulent online stores, and suspicious security alerts. Using a standardized rubric, the study compared each model's threat recognition, safety recommendations, cybersecurity knowledge, clarity, and reliability. The findings highlight conversational AI's potential to improve cybersecurity awareness while also showing limitations in the accuracy, accessibility, and reliability of AI-generated security advice. The study emphasizes the importance of independent verification and human judgment when using AI to navigate online threats.

Abstract This theoretical article examines artificial intelligence in organizational digitalization. It distinguishes digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation, then combines sociotechnical theory with the dynamic capabilities perspective to explain how technology interacts with employees, routines, organizational structures and adaptation. The framework proposes that artificial intelligence supports transformation when aligned with strategy, integrated into processes and complemented by employee expertise, data and responsible governance. It highlights tensions involving discretion, bias, accountability and the fit between standardized systems and local practices. The article contributes propositions for empirical research and argues that AI’s value depends on integrating technical systems with human capabilities and organizational oversight. AI applications can automate repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, personalize services and support decisions. However, their effects depend on data quality, employee skills, leadership commitment and the organizational context. For this reason, the article moves the focus beyond the simple adoption of AI and highlights the organizational capabilities and governance needed to integrate it responsibly. Keywords: artificial intelligence; organizational digitalization; digital transformation; dynamic capabilities; sociotechnical systems; AI adoption; responsible AI governance.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents one of the most transformative technological advancements of the 21st century. AI is rapidly transforming human societies and their knowledge transfer systems. While AI’s immediate impacts are currently widely monitored and studied on a broad basis, its implications for the intergenerational compound in society remain underexplored. This chapter investigates how AI innovations reshape intergenerational knowledge creation, transfer, and preservation. Drawing on theories of knowledge management, organizational learning, and intergenerational equity, the chapter conceptualizes AI as an agent of innovation and cultural continuity. Case studies on climate change mitigation, sustainable development, and digital legacy highlight the potentials and risks of AI in fostering intergenerational knowledge flows. The analysis underscores both the benefits of AI – such as enhanced cultural transmission, digital legacies, and novel forms of intergenerational literacy – as well as the costs, including sustainability concerns, cultural homogenization, and ethical dilemmas. The research outcomes cover the use of AI for intergenerational transfers. Positive potentials but also potential downfalls of AI in society in regard to the intergenerational compound will be discussed. The chapter concludes with recommendations for responsible governance frameworks that ensure AI-driven intergenerational knowledge transfer remains equitable, sustainable, and inclusive.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) does not constitute a single phenomenon in archival practice. It may generate potential records, support archival functions, assist tool development, analyze holdings, become an object of preservation, or mediate access. Treating these different modes of involvement as homogeneous produces imprecise diagnoses and inadequate safeguards. This theoretical-conceptual article proposes a six-mode model: AI-assisted record production, AI tools for archival functions, AI-assisted tool development, AI analysis of archival holdings, AI systems as preservation objects, and AI-mediated access. Each mode is evaluated against common requirements of archival trust — authenticity, reliability, accuracy, and the chain of preservation — and is subject to a cross-cutting governance framework based on paradata, explainable AI, bias mitigation, ethical use, and accountable human oversight. The analysis is guided by the theoretical-methodological framework of InterPARES, particularly InterPARES Trust AI (2021–2026). The article concludes that AI can support archival work only when its use is governed by archival principles, documented procedures, and clearly assigned human and institutional responsibility. The model provides an instrument for analyzing AI initiatives, designing safeguards, and guiding future empirical validation through case studies.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence now touches most stages of teaching and learning. Learning analytics predicts which students are at risk, knowledge tracing models estimate what each student has mastered, intelligent tutors adapt practice to the learner, and large language models can explain, grade and write. The same tools have created new problems. Generative AI makes it easy to submit text that a student did not write, detection tools are unreliable, and models trained on student data raise questions of privacy and fairness. The problem is that these topics are reviewed in separate literatures: analytics and tutoring surveys rarely discuss academic integrity, and integrity studies rarely discuss the learning models that produce or detect the text. This review brings them into one framework of five layers: learning analytics and prediction, personalization and intelligent tutoring, generative AI in learning, academic integrity, and a cross-cutting layer of privacy, fairness and inclusion. It organizes 42 studies and compares their methods and reported results. Deep knowledge tracing raised the area under the curve from 0.67 to 0.86 over Bayesian knowledge tracing, and intelligent tutoring systems raised test scores by a median of 0.66 standard deviations. A randomized trial found that a carefully designed AI tutor produced learning gains of 0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations over in-class active learning, but a field experiment found that unrestricted GPT-4 access raised practice grades by 48% and then lowered exam grades by 17%. Detection of AI-generated text is weak: tested tools were neither accurate nor reliable, and detectors flagged 61% of essays by non-native English writers as machine-written. Few studies connect personalization with integrity or measure bias across student groups. Future work should design AI tutors with learning safeguards, assess integrity through process rather than detection alone, and evaluate both under privacy protection and across diverse learners.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in education to support learning, teaching, assessm ent, and academ ic adm inistration. Exam ples include adaptive learning system s, intelligent tutoring tools, autom ated feedback, learning analytics, and generative AI assistants. This paper review s selected published research and international guidance to exam ine the potential benefits, m ajor risks, and future directions of AI in education. The literature indicates that AI can support personalized learning, provide tim ely feedback, assist educators w ith planning, and im prove access to learning support. A t the sam e tim e, its use raises concerns about privacy, bias, accuracy, unequal access, academ ic integrity, and over-reliance on autom ated system s. This paper uses a narrative literature-review approach rather than reporting a new experim ent or student survey. It concludes that AI should support— not replace— educators and learners, and that responsible adoption requires transparency, data protection, teacher preparation, hum an oversight, and evaluation in real educational settings.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study addresses the following research question: What are the implications of artificial intelligence (AI) for Personalized Learning and Online Higher Education (OHE)? Design/methodology/approach A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews including faculty members and higher education administrators. The data were analyzed to identify the adoption factors, challenges, opportunities, and ethical considerations. An Integrative Model of Adopting AI in Online Higher Education (IMAOHE) was developed based on the empirical findings. Findings AI supports personalized learning through adaptive assessment, real-time feedback, learning analytics, and tailored content. The reported challenges include ethical dilemmas, institutional barriers, and the need to preserve teacher autonomy. Research limitations/implications Limited respondents and lack of student perspectives suggest future research with larger, more diverse samples and mixed-methods or longitudinal designs. Practical implications The model guides institutions, educators, and developers to integrate AI ethically and strategically, ensuring meaningful, context-aware learning. Social implications AI can enhance equity, inclusion, and student-centered learning while maintaining human mediation and cultural sensitivity. Originality/value This study provides an empirically grounded model linking AI adoption to pedagogical personalization in OHE, offering actionable insights for ethical and effective AI integration.

documents.abstract: This repository contains the supplementary data and materials supporting the systematic review entitled “Artificial Intelligence in Higher Mathematics Education: A Systematic Review and Evidence-Informed Framework for Productive Pedagogical Integration and Human–AI Interaction” by Felix O. Egara and Alfred M. Msomi. The review synthesises empirical research published between January 2021 and September 2026 on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher mathematics education. Searches were conducted in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection, and 18 studies meeting the eligibility criteria were included in the review. The repository contains the original database search exports, the merged bibliographic dataset, the PRISMA 2020 reporting checklist, the full search strategies and eligibility criteria, the evidence-to-framework synthesis matrix, and the study characteristics and data-extraction matrix. These materials document the review’s information sources, study selection, data extraction, and evidence synthesis. They are intended to support transparency, methodological reporting, and further scholarly engagement with research on AI-supported mathematics learning in higher education.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as an important technology in modern healthcare and is gradually changing the way hospital pharmacy services are delivered. In hospital pharmacy practice, AI can support pharmacists in activities such as prescription screening, medication error detection, drug interaction checking, adverse drug reaction monitoring, inventory management, antimicrobial stewardship, drug information services, and personalized patient care. By processing large amounts of clinical and pharmaceutical data, AI-based systems can help identify potential medication-related problems more quickly and support pharmacists in making informed decisions. AI can also improve the efficiency of drug procurement, stock forecasting, dispensing, and medication-use processes, thereby reducing workload and improving patient safety. However, the implementation of AI also presents challenges, including data privacy and security, inaccurate or biased outputs, limited transparency of algorithms, integration with existing hospital systems, financial costs, and the need for trained healthcare professionals. Therefore, AI should be considered a supportive technology rather than a replacement for pharmacists. Effective collaboration between AI systems and pharmacy professionals, along with appropriate ethical, legal, and regulatory frameworks, will be essential for its safe and responsible use. This review discusses the current applications, benefits, challenges, ethical and legal considerations, and future potential of AI in hospital pharmacy practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into modern healthcare, supporting diagnostic interpretation, clinical decision-making, workflow optimization, documentation, patient communication, medical education, and outcome prediction. This narrative review examines the current clinical applications and future directions of healthcare AI, with radiology presented as a model specialty because of its standardized workflows, large datasets, and measurable outputs. It discusses the growing roles of generative AI, large language models, multimodal foundation models, patient-facing applications, and AI-assisted medical education, while emphasizing persistent limitations such as hallucinations, bias, limited generalizability, inadequate reporting, and insufficient prospective clinical evidence. Emerging approaches, including digital twins and agentic AI systems, may enable patient-specific simulation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-step workflow automation; however, their clinical use remains at an early stage. Successful implementation will require external validation, transparent reporting, continuous performance monitoring, institutional governance, and clearly defined human oversight. The future value of AI will therefore depend not on complete autonomy, but on its ability to improve healthcare safely, effectively, equitably, and responsibly within human-supervised clinical systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping every stage of the medicine life cycle, from the identification of drug targets to the counselling of patients at the pharmacy counter. This review examines how AI technologies, chiefly machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing and generative models, are applied across pharmaceutical science and pharmacy practice, and weighs the opportunities they offer against the challenges that limit their safe adoption. In drug discovery, AI supports target identification, protein structure prediction, virtual screening, de novo molecular design, retrosynthesis, drug repurposing and clinical trial optimisation. In pharmaceutics and manufacturing, it is used to predict formulation behaviour, guide three-dimensional printing of dosage forms and enable real-time process control. In clinical, hospital and community pharmacy, AI-enabled tools assist prescription verification, prevention of adverse drug events, dose individualisation, adherence support, inventory management and patient communication. AI also strengthens pharmacovigilance, regulatory science and pharmacy education. The principal opportunities are shorter development timelines, lower attrition, personalised therapy, safer medication use and more efficient operations. The principal challenges are poor data quality and bias, limited transparency of complex models, privacy, unclear accountability, evolving regulation, validation gaps, fabricated output from language models and the need to prepare the pharmacy workforce. We conclude that AI is best viewed as a decision-support partner that extends, and does not replace, the professional judgement of pharmacists and pharmaceutical scientists, and we outline priorities for responsible implementation. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Machine learning; Deep learning; Drug discovery; Pharmacy practice; Pharmacovigilance; Personalised medicine; Pharmaceutical manufacturing.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition whose diagnosis still rests on clinical interviews and rating scales, and whose treatment is limited by partial response to medication, side effects, and unequal access to behavioural care. Artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) in particular, has been proposed as a way to make diagnosis more objective and treatment more personalised and scalable. This review summarises the current state of that evidence. In diagnosis, ML models trained on neuroimaging, electroencephalography (EEG), and behavioural or sensor data frequently report high accuracy, but results vary widely across datasets, are rarely validated externally, and have not yet produced a tool that clinicians can rely on. In treatment, the strongest evidence concerns a prescription digital therapeutic delivered as a video game-like intervention, whereas computerised cognitive training and neurofeedback show limited effects on blinded measures of ADHD symptoms. Key barriers are non-representative training data, algorithmic bias, privacy, weak regulatory and reporting standards, and the risk that predictive accuracy is mistaken for clinical utility. We conclude that AI is best positioned as decision support within a clinician-led, hybrid model of care, and we outline the research needed to move from promising prototypes to validated practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The pharmaceutical sector is dealing with a number of issues, such as growing R&D expenses, protracted drug development schedules, complicated regulations, supply chain interruptions, and heightened rivalry in the market. The development of new drugs is very resource intensive and often requires years of effort and billions of dollars as well as a high rate of clinical trial failures. The stringent regulatory requirements that demand extensive data validation and compliance further prolong the market entry process. There are also major issues related to counterfeit drugs and poor supply chain practice that are threats to both the business and the public. Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the answers that can solve these problems with a change. AI-powered drug discovery cuts down on the time and expense involved with conventional methods by speeding up the identification of possible molecules. Machine learning algorithms can also help inform clinical trial designs and improve rates of successful trials by selecting the right patient population and predicting outcomes. AI-powered automation enhances compliance with regulations and ensures all documents are accurate and up to standard. AI can also help to predict demand, detect irregularities, and optimize logistics, minimizing the risk of shortages and counterfeit goods in manufacturing and supply chain management. Additionally, AI-powered personalized medicine reduces side effects and increases therapeutic efficacy by customizing therapies for each patient. Adoption of AI is hampered by issues including data protection, compatibility with existing systems, and governmental approval, despite its potential. With further advancements in AI, however, the pharmaceutical industry could benefit from increased involvement in addressing challenges, leading to improved patient outcomes, more efficient drug development, and better operational efficiency.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background:AI is being increasingly investigated as a clinical decision support tool for ED triage and acute-care prioritization. Machine-learning, deep-learning, natural language processing (NLP) and large language model systems have shown good predictive performance but concerns remain about under-triage, over-triage, generalizability, workflow integration and implementation safety. We systematically reviewed the accuracy, safety and implementation readiness of AI-driven clinical decision-support systems for ED triage.Methods:This review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane Library were searched (citation chaining, reference-list screening and recent systematic reviews were also used). Of the 1076 records identified, 312 duplicates were removed and 764 records screened; 79 full-text reports were assessed and 65 excluded; fourteen studies were included in narrative synthesis. Meta-analysis was not performed because populations, AI architectures, triage systems, reference standards and outcome metrics are highly heterogeneous.Results:Conventional machine learning, gradient boosting, neural networks, deep learning, natural language processing and large language models were included in the studies. AI systems generally outperformed conventional triage for critical illness prediction (hospitalization), intensive-care admission and mortality; reported AUROCs for early mortality were 0.962 and for 30-day mortality 0.925. Direct triage systems also had some success: KATE had 75.7% ESI assignment accuracy; prospective GPT-4 and GPT-4o studieshad κ = 0.899 and multicenter κ = 0.833 with F1 = 0.897 agreement with expert triage but safety outcomes under-triage/over-triage subgroup performance and patient-important outcomes were inconsistently reported.Conclusions:ED triage systems powered by AI have great potential as supervised clinical decision support tools but not yet enough evidence to justify autonomous deployment. Prospective multicenter validation, standardized safety metrics, subgroup analysis, workflow evaluation, governance and post-deployment monitoring are needed before widespread implementation
